definition: Developmental robotics (DevRob), sometimes called epigenetic robotics, is a scientific field which aims at studying the developmental mechanisms, architectures and constraints that allow lifelong and open-ended learning of new skills and new knowledge in embodied machines.
details: As in human children, learning is expected to be cumulative and of progressively increasing complexity, and to result from self-exploration of the world in combination with social interaction. The typical methodological approach consists in starting from theories of human and animal development elaborated in fields such as developmental psychology, neuroscience, developmental and evolutionary biology, and linguistics, then to formalize and implement them in robots, sometimes exploring extensions or variants of them. The experimentation of those models in robots allows researchers to confront them with reality, and as a consequence, developmental robotics also provides feedback and novel hypotheses on theories of human and animal development. Developmental robotics is related to but differs from evolutionary robotics (ER). ER uses populations of robots that evolve over time, whereas DevRob is interested in how the organization of a single robot's control system develops through experience, over time. DevRob is also related to work done in the domains of robotics and artificial life.

explainer.lead: Developmental robotics studies how a robot could build skills gradually through its own experience, much as a child does. It matters because lifelong, open-ended learning requires more than training a machine for one fixed task: the machine must keep reorganizing what it knows as new abilities become possible.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot learning a bit like a child: it tries things, sees what happens, and learns from playing and interacting with people. Each new skill can help it learn a harder one later. Researchers also watch these robot experiments to get new ideas about how children and animals develop.
tiers.practitioner: A developmental-robotics project starts with a theory from psychology, neuroscience, biology, or linguistics, formalizes it, and implements it in an embodied robot. The design should support cumulative learning through self-exploration and social interaction, with later skills building on earlier ones. A key pitfall is confusing changes in one robot's controller through experience with evolutionary robotics, which changes a population across generations.
tiers.paperLevel: Developmental robotics studies the mechanisms, architectures, and constraints enabling lifelong, open-ended acquisition of skills and knowledge in embodied machines. If C_t denotes one robot's control organization at time t, development concerns how C_t changes through cumulative experience, rather than how a population of controllers evolves. Robot experiments test formalized theories of human and animal development against physical reality and can generate feedback and new hypotheses for those theories.

explainer.example: Imagine a robot that first moves its arm and observes the outcomes, then learns to direct its hand toward an object. That reaching ability can support later object-handling practice, while social interaction supplies additional learning opportunities; the same robot's controller develops throughout, rather than a population of robots evolving.

explainer.intuition: Instead of giving a robot every ability in advance, let simple abilities emerge first and become building blocks for harder ones. Exploration of the world and interaction with other people drive this gradual development.
howItWorks: Start with a theory of human or animal development.
Turn the theory into a formal model and implement it in a robot.
Let the robot gain experience through self-exploration and social interaction.
Build increasingly complex skills cumulatively as its control system develops.
Use the experimental results to test the model and suggest refinements to developmental theories.
explainer.whyItMatters: The field connects two goals: building machines that can keep learning beyond a fixed task, and testing scientific theories of development in physical systems. A robot's failures and successes can reveal assumptions that are hard to examine through theory alone.
misconceptions: It is not evolutionary robotics: DevRob concerns experience-driven development in one robot, not evolution across a population.
It is not simply ordinary robot learning: its focus is cumulative, progressively more complex, lifelong and open-ended development.
It does not only borrow from developmental science; robot experiments can also feed new hypotheses back into that science.
